title: Acheulean hand axe

source.author: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (model by Kay Waller)
source.notes: Photogrammetry scan of a real flint hand axe, catalogue 516a5, published CC0 by UNC's Research Laboratories of Archaeology on Sketchfab (https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/acheulean-hand-axe-516a5-ab5a9c0862974e2b99a951ac4776257e, uid ab5a9c0862974e2b99a951ac4776257e, user rla-archaeology) and mirrored as a glb on Zenodo ('Source: Objaverse 1.0 / Sketchfab', DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21530762); anonymous download verified. The RLA description gives the findspot as 'Montieres Amiens, France'; the old collector's ink label visible on the scan reads 'AMIENS - ST. ACHEUL ... Ach. 516A5', i.e. the Acheulean type site (Montières and Saint-Acheul are quarters of Amiens). Raw glb: 60,000 triangles, one texture, bounding box 2.6514 x 1.0572 x 1.5256 units; real length 99.3 mm, so scale = 0.0993/2.6514 = 0.03745 m per unit. Use the raw '<uid>.glb', not the '_normalized' variants. Dimensions (99.3 x 60.6 x 31.4 mm), material and 'Lower Paleolithic (before 300,000 years ago)' from the RLA description; the broader Acheulean range (c. 1.6 million to 100,000 years ago) from Wikipedia 'Hand axe'. Collected 1929 by James Bell Bullitt, donated to UNC. No Smithsonian/Met scan found.

object.description: The hand axe is the signature tool of the Acheulean, a tradition that early humans sustained for well over a million years across Africa, Europe and Asia. Each one was shaped by striking flakes from both faces of a flint nodule until a symmetrical, teardrop cutting edge remained. This example comes from the gravel pits of Saint-Acheul at Amiens, the site that gave the industry its name, and still bears its 1920s collector's label.
facts: The Acheulean is named after Saint-Acheul, a suburb of Amiens, where hand axes were found in the Somme river gravels in the 19th century.
Hand axes were made from roughly 1.6 million to about 100,000 years ago, chiefly by Homo erectus and its successors, and only rarely by Homo sapiens.
Jacques Boucher de Perthes's finds in the Somme gravels in the 1840s helped establish that humans had coexisted with extinct Ice Age animals.

tour: A hand axe from Saint-Acheul, 300,000 years old. Someone chose this shape and worked stone to it, and so did a thousand generations after.
